title: Comparing the size of penguin species
text:
Data: Palmer Penguins, Palmer Station Antarctica LTER.
Load Libraries
First we will load in pandas, matplotlib and palmerpenguins for our analysis of the penguins dataset.

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from palmerpenguins import load_penguins

Looking at the data set
First, lets take a look at the dataset to see what we are working with.

penguins = load_penguins()
print(penguins.head())

print([species for species, _ in penguins.groupby("species")])

  species     island  bill_length_mm  bill_depth_mm  flipper_length_mm  \
0  Adelie  Torgersen            39.1           18.7              181.0   
1  Adelie  Torgersen            39.5           17.4              186.0   
2  Adelie  Torgersen            40.3           18.0              195.0   
3  Adelie  Torgersen             NaN            NaN                NaN   
4  Adelie  Torgersen            36.7           19.3              193.0   

   body_mass_g     sex  year  
0       3750.0    male  2007  
1       3800.0  female  2007  
2       3250.0  female  2007  
3          NaN     NaN  2007  
4       3450.0  female  2007  
['Adelie', 'Chinstrap', 'Gentoo']


The data set includes 3 different species: Adelie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo penguins. There are entries for the penguins bills, flippers, origin, sex and measurement year.
What are we analyzing
We will be analyzing the size differences between different species of penguins. The purpose of this analysis is to see if penguin species differ enough in size to visually distinguish the species simply based on physical measurements.

penguins_grouped = penguins.groupby("species")
for species, group in penguins_grouped:
    print(f"{species:<15} {len(group)}")

Adelie          152
Chinstrap       68
Gentoo          124


The most sampled species in the dataset is the Adelie species, followed by the Gentoo and the Chinstrap species.
Visualization of Species Sizes
Now, we can do a visual comparison of the species by plotting.

fig, axs = plt.subplots()

for species, group in penguins_grouped:
    axs.scatter(group["bill_length_mm"], group["body_mass_g"], label = species)

axs.set_xlabel("Bill Length (mm)")
axs.set_ylabel("Body Mass (g)")
axs.legend(title = "Species")

plt.show()







Figure 1: Comparing bill length and body mass for penguin species





We can observe a clear trend in the visual. Adelie penguins are on average, smaller on all metrics compared to Chinstrap and Gentoo. Gentoo penguins are larger than both Chinstrap and Adelie penguins in body mass, but have similar bill length to Chinstrap penguins. Therefore, it is possible to identify each of these species simply based on physical factors, however there is some overlap.

title: Comparing sizing of human and non-human species in Star Wars
text:
Data: Star Wars API, via dplyr package
Load Libraries
First we will load in the dplyr and ggplot2 libraries for our analysis of the Star Wars dataset.

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

What are we analyzing
We will be analyzing the size differences between humans and non-human species in the Star Wars films. The purpose of this analysis is to determine if non-human species in the films follow real world (human-like) proportions. Here, we split the starwars dataset into Human and other species to see how the data is distributed.

count_human <- starwars |>
  filter(!is.na(height), !is.na(mass)) |>
  mutate(binary_species = case_when(
    species == "Human" ~ "Human",
    TRUE ~ "Other"
  )) |>
  count(binary_species)

count_human

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  binary_species     n
  <chr>          <int>
1 Human             20
2 Other             39


There are almost double the amount of non-human species to humans. This makes sense as there are many different species grouped into non-human.
Visualization of Human to Non-human Proportions
Now, we will plot human character sizes against non-human character sizes to visually identify any differences.
NOTE: there was one non-human character skewing the graph, so it was removed as an outlier. We will get to this later.

starwars |>
  filter(!is.na(height), !is.na(mass), mass < 1000) |>
  mutate(binary_species = case_when(
    species == "Human" ~ "Human",
    TRUE ~ "Other"
  )) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = height, y = mass, color = binary_species)) + geom_point()







Figure 1: Comparison of Human to Non-human Character Size in Starwars Films





We can observe a clear cluster in the center of human and other. This cluster is between heights of 150 to 200 centimeters and mass of 70 to 90 kg. However, we can note that there are many species that are not human which are much smaller than typical human height and mass, and also some non-human species which extend much beyond the maximum human height. Therefore, we can conclude that non-human species in the series do not strictly follow human sizing.
What was the outlier?
Below we determine which character had an extreme value for mass, extending much beyond any other characters.

filtered_out <- starwars |>
  filter(mass > 1000) |>
  slice(1)

filtered_out

# A tibble: 1 × 14
  name      height  mass hair_color skin_color eye_color birth_year sex   gender
  <chr>      <int> <dbl> <chr>      <chr>      <chr>          <dbl> <chr> <chr> 
1 Jabba De…    175  1358 <NA>       green-tan… orange           600 herm… mascu…
# ℹ 5 more variables: homeworld <chr>, species <chr>, films <list>,
#   vehicles <list>, starships <list>


The character was Jabba Desilijic Tiure which is a Hutt (non-human) species with an astonishing mass of 1358 kg!
